settings.eyebrow: A theoretical response to agent-harness inefficiency
settings.headline:
The agent that never loses
the plot.
Kairos.
settings.copy: Every agent harness today spends a large share of its attention managing itself — compacting context, re-deriving state, second-guessing its own work. Kairos reorganizes the harness so the model only ever thinks about the task, never about surviving the session.

stats.label: Of tokens often spent re-deriving state

settings.title: The job of a harness is not to maximize what an agent can
settings.title_after: — it is to minimize how much of its attention is spent managing itself.
settings.image_caption: The opportune moment — work dispatched exactly when it is ready

paragraphs.text: Research across Hermes Agent, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Devin, and the open-source harness layer converges on a single conclusion: the frontier models have largely converged, and the wrapper now decides the experience.

And the wrappers share seven expensive habits — leaking context, sessions that forget, one-shotting, soft self-review, stale plans, tool-call round-trip overhead, and hidden harness control. None of these are model weaknesses. They are architectural choices that Kairos proposes to reverse.

settings.quote: You never compact a ledger; you query it.

settings.title: Why today's agents burn their
settings.intro: These are harness-level inefficiencies, present across the current generation of agent tools. Each one is a place where attention is spent on the harness itself instead of on the work.

features.title: Context is a leaking bucket
features.text: Compaction summarizes away the exact granular state a later bug needs. Even the best compression is lossy, and context anxiety makes agents wrap up early near a limit they believe is near.

features.title: Sessions forget
features.text: Each context window begins with no memory. Agents re-explore, re-run, and re-guess what a handoff should have carried. Memory files help but depend on the agent deciding to consult them.

features.title: One-shotting & premature completion
features.text: Agents try to eat the whole task in one pass, run out of context, and leave a half-built mess — or see progress and mistake it for completion on a feature that never ran end-to-end.
features.detail: The field patches this with prompts, not structure

features.title: Self-review is soft
features.text: The same weights that generated the output now judge it. The result is confident praise of mediocre work. A separate evaluator helps but doubles the inference budget.

features.title: Plans go stale — or are over-administered
features.text: Task trees anchor an agent to a plan reality has invalidated, or decompose so finely that more tokens go to bookkeeping than to the work. Checkbox theater replaces progress.

features.title: Tool-call round-trip overhead
features.text: Every tool call re-sends the system prompt, schemas, and a growing transcript. Progressive-disclosure helps, but the reason-act-observe loop itself is the largest single token sink.

features.title: Hidden harness control
features.text: Many harnesses mutate context, prompts, and tools in ways the user cannot inspect or steer. The field's answer is user-owned minimal harnesses — but the burden lands on the operator.

settings.title: Five structural bets,
settings.intro: Where today's harnesses add patches (compaction, feature lists, evaluator agents, memory files), Kairos moves those responsibilities out of the model's reasoning loop and into deterministic, inspectable harness layers.

design.title: Split attention
design.text: Separate the working set (active task) from the ledger (all prior state). The model's window holds only the current task, a fresh situation card, and the artifacts for the immediate decision.

design.title: Typed state ledger
design.text: History lives as typed, queryable records — values, error signatures, decisions with reasons — not prose. The harness rewrites the situation card deterministically between steps. You query the past; you never carry it.

design.title: Opportune dispatch
design.text: Continuously score readiness: task specified, inputs fresh, verification cheap. Spend inference only at the task's opportune moment — never guessing early, never acting on stale state.

build.title: Verification is a guarantee
build.text: Schedule verification as a typed step with its own toolset and a skeptical evaluator — a different model family than the generator — run against the live artifact, not a summary.

build.title: Stateless subagents
build.text: Subagents write results into the shared ledger (not a prose summary) and return a pointer + diff. Async results carry their context ID, so reconciliation is deterministic.

build.title: Radical transparency
build.text: Every context mutation, compaction decision, ledger write, and dispatch decision is observable, inspectable, and overridable. The user owns the harness, not the vendor.

launch.title: A theoretical response
launch.text: Kairos is a design thesis, not a shipped system. It is a second-generation opinion on how the next harness should be built, informed by the failure modes this generation exposed.

launch.title: Informed by Hermes' strengths
launch.text: Hermes' structured compaction, progressive-disclosure skills, and FTS5 session search are genuinely strong — they would be inputs to Kairos' ledger, not things to discard.

launch.title: Honest about its costs
launch.text: A typed ledger needs deterministic state extraction. Readiness scoring is domain-dependent. Separate-model evaluators double spend. These remain open, unproven claims.

settings.title: The harness you can
settings.image_caption: A live context-health console — observability as a first-class surface

paragraphs.text: Transparency is not a feature Kairos adds; it is the substrate. Every decision the harness makes — a dispatch, a ledger write, a verification schedule — appears in a live console as an inspectable, revertible action.
This is the OpenDev 'transparency over magic' principle made a product surface, not a buried mechanic. The operator owns the harness the same way they own their terminal.

settings.title: From intake to verified handoff,

steps.title: Intake & classify
steps.text: A task arrives and is typed: is it specified, are inputs available, is verification cheap? If not ready, it waits — it is never handed to the model half-formed.

steps.title: Dispatch at the moment
steps.text: The readiness score crosses its threshold and the task is dispatched. The model receives only the current task, the fresh situation card, and the exact artifacts it needs.

steps.title: Execute with a live card
steps.text: The harness rewrites the situation card deterministically between steps. The model never carries the past; the ledger does, and the card is always current.

steps.title: Verify as a guarantee
steps.text: A skeptical evaluator, a different model family, runs against the live artifact. 'Done' is a verifiable condition, not a self-assessment.

steps.title: Ledger write & handoff
steps.text: Results and diffs are written to the typed ledger. The next session queries state instead of re-deriving it. No cold start, no lossy summary.

settings.note: Kairos is a design thesis — the readiness scoring function and the ledger-extraction layer are the two hardest, least-proven pieces.

settings.heading: Want the full thesis?
settings.description: The complete research write-up — the seven inefficiencies, the five pillars, and the honest caveats — is documented in the Kairos concept file.

settings.title: Questions, answered
settings.intro: The honest, unpolished answers to the obvious questions about a concept product.

items.question: Is Kairos a real product I can install?
items.answer: No. Kairos is a theoretical response and design thesis — a second-generation opinion on how an agent harness should be architected. No shipped code yet.

items.question: How does it relate to Hermes Agent?
items.answer: Kairos is informed by Hermes' strengths — structured compaction, progressive-disclosure skills, FTS5 session search — and proposes to take them further by moving state out of the window into a typed ledger.

items.question: What's the hardest part to actually build?
items.answer: Two pieces: deterministically extracting typed state from model output into the ledger, and defining a readiness-scoring function that reliably knows when a task is truly 'ripe.'

items.question: Doesn't a separate evaluator double the cost?
items.answer: Yes. That is a real, admitted trade-off. The claim is that enforced verification catches failures that soft self-review misses — but the cost objection is legitimate and unproven either way.

settings.title: Discuss the thesis
settings.intro: If you are building an agent harness — or just tired of one that loses the plot — Kairos is a starting point for the conversation.

settings.blurb: A theoretical agent harness that reorganizes attention so the model only ever thinks about the task — never about surviving the session.
